body: Thirty years he has lived in this country, and at nearly three in the morning he is on a plastic chair in a corridor outside a set of double doors, a man in his fifties with a paper cup he has not drunk. He has been there two hours. He writes reports in English, argues in English, and explained his wife’s medication twice tonight in English better than the form had room for. At some point he stops looking at the doors and puts his forehead on his hands, and what comes out, barely aloud, is not English. It is four or five words in the language his mother used in her kitchen, and he says them over and over, and is not aware of having chosen them.
Nobody decides that. It is not a preference and it is not loyalty to anything. Under a certain weight a person goes to the language underneath the others, and it turns out there is one.

People who live between two languages will tell you they are slightly different people in each. Not less capable — different. There is one they argue in, one they count in, and one they would swear in if something fell on their foot, and those are frequently not the same.

Prayer belongs with the last of those, and the reason is not what people assume. A language is learned in rooms, and the rooms teach it what it is for. The second language is usually learned at a school desk, a counter, an interview, a ward — places where a person is being assessed and had better be composed. It arrives equipped for competence and badly equipped for collapse. The first was learned in a kitchen by somebody already on your side. Fluency turns out to be the wrong measure. You can be perfectly fluent in a language and still not be able to be honest in it, because you learned it in rooms where honesty was not what was being asked for.

This dial carries 40 international frequencies across 29 languages, out of 121 stations. Each is hosted in its own language rather than subtitled into it, and each keeps its own hours rather than a translated copy of somebody else’s.

Both halves of that are expensive and the second is the one people miss. Hosting in a language means hosts who work in it, a repertoire from where the language came from, and prayer hours set where they fall for the people who keep them rather than for a head office. It would be far cheaper to run one schedule and lay voices over it. It is not done that way because a translated prayer arrives after the fact, and a man at three in the morning has nothing spare to wait with.

The habit of treating this as a solved problem runs deep, and it is not stupid. The church has a working common language now, more or less, and it has done enormous good: conferences happen, books travel, a pastor in one country learns from one in another by Tuesday. What that efficiency conceals is that it works best on the part of faith that behaves like information. Doctrine travels well. Argument travels well. What does not travel is the register a person uses when they have run out of composure, and that register is no detail at the edge of the faith. It is most of what prayer consists of.

It is worth noticing how this was arranged the one time it was arranged directly. The account of Pentecost is not that everybody suddenly understood one language, which would have been simpler and cheaper to administer for ever afterwards. It is that each person heard in the language they were born into. That is a costly decision, taken deliberately, at the founding, in front of witnesses — and it says something that a common tongue was available and was not used.
So the question is not whether a person can pray in their second language. Of course they can.

It is worth being fair to the other side, because the case is real. People pray in acquired languages constantly and God is not at the door checking grammar; missionaries have done it for centuries and something clearly happened. Plenty of believers have no first language left to return to, and plenty of second-generation families pray in the country’s language and mean it. None of that is in doubt. The narrower claim is about what a broadcast can do for somebody alone at an hour when they are managing nothing. A prayer handed to you in your working language gives you something to follow; the same prayer in the language underneath gives you something to join. Those are not the same act, and the difference shows up precisely when a person is too tired to perform.
A prayer you have to translate is a prayer with a delay in it.

A young man in a shared flat gets in from a night shift at about twenty to six and makes tea before the others are up, and normally puts nothing on because he does not want to wake anybody. One morning he puts a station on very low, in Arabic, because it was the first thing he found and he was too tired to look further. A woman is singing something with the long open vowels his grandmother’s church used. He waits for the kettle with his hands flat on the worktop. When he notices what he is doing, several minutes later, he has been praying — in Arabic, out loud, in his own kitchen, which he has not done since he left home and never decided to start again.
That is the mechanism, and it is not mysterious. He did not choose to pray. He was handed a sound his mouth already knew, at an hour when he had nothing left to keep up, and the rest did itself.

There is a cost and it should be stated without softening. A person who prays best in a language their children do not speak has a real problem, and a frequency will not solve it. It can widen the gap in a household. It can pull somebody away from the congregation they attend, where they are known, towards a broadcast that speaks better to one part of them and cannot visit them in hospital. And the mother tongue does not only carry the kitchen. It carries whatever else was said in it.

None of which argues for smoothing the language away. It argues the opposite. A language that can still hurt you is a language that still has access to you, and access is the whole of what is at issue. The tongue carrying the worst things anybody said to you is the same tongue that can carry a psalm past the part of you that manages everything — which is why it is worth having somewhere to hear it, and why the sound of it at twenty to six does what no translation can.

So the argument comes down to a narrow point about hours and access. The international frequencies on this band are hosted in their own languages, not translated into them afterwards, and they run at the hours when people are awake and alone with something rather than at hours borrowed from another time zone. That is not a nicety, and not a gesture to anybody’s heritage. It is the difference between a prayer somebody observes and a prayer somebody joins.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The band carries four kinds of programming and it helps to know they are there. There is music, which is most of it — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to leave running with children in the room. And there is the international band, where each language holds its own number, hosts and clock. 46 stations are on air, and every one is already playing rather than waiting to be asked what you are in the mood for.

If Arabic is the language underneath yours, start at HM 328.70 — Inspire Crown. It is the Arabic-language flagship of this band, and it is the right recommendation here for one reason above the others: its two anchors are prayer hours, not shows. Tasbeha Sabah in the morning and Tasbeha Masaa in the evening sit at the ends of an Arabic day rather than somebody else’s, and Amir Inspire hosts them in Arabic rather than reading a translation. It carries Coptic, Maronite and Levantine tradition alongside modern worship — the sound your grandmother’s church made and the sound your cousins make now, on one number that does not move. If your language is another, the band holds 40 of these and the argument is unchanged.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download, no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. Add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which languages people reach for at which hours — which is how the next prayer hour, and the next language, get put on the air.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Put HM 328.70 on very low tomorrow, at whatever hour of yours is the one where you have nothing left to keep up, then get on with the kettle and leave it alone. You are not being asked to evaluate a language service. You are being asked to find out what comes out of you when nobody is translating anything, which is not a thing you will learn by thinking about it.
